name: Validity, Repeatability, Reproducibility and Logbooks
what: This subtopic covers what makes an experiment valid, the difference between repeatability and reproducibility, and the purpose and contents of an experimental logbook. These concepts link experimental design to the quality and trustworthiness of the results obtained.
why: Even a carefully executed experiment can produce meaningless data if the design is flawed or if the method cannot be replicated. Understanding validity, repeatability and reproducibility is what separates reliable science from one-off results that cannot be trusted.

items.title: I can explain what makes an experiment valid
items.what: A valid experiment is one that actually measures what it intends to measure. Validity requires only one independent variable to be changed at a time, appropriate controlled variables, suitable equipment, and unbiased data collection and analysis.
items.why: If an experiment is not valid, the results cannot be used to draw meaningful conclusions about the relationship being investigated. Invalid experiments waste time and resources, and can lead to incorrect or misleading findings.
items.example: An experiment testing how light intensity affects photocurrent is invalid if the experimenter also changes the colour (wavelength) of the light between trials, because this introduces a second independent variable.

items.title: I can distinguish between repeatability and reproducibility
items.what: Repeatability refers to how closely results agree when the same experimenter repeats the same experiment under the same conditions. Reproducibility refers to how closely results agree when a different experimenter repeats the experiment, possibly with different equipment.
items.why: Repeatability confirms that the results are consistent within a single experimental context. Reproducibility is a stronger test: it confirms that the findings are not specific to one lab, one set of equipment, or one experimenter's technique.
items.example: If a student measures the same spring constant three times in their own lab and gets consistent results, the experiment is repeatable. If a student at a different school uses their own equipment and gets a similar value, the result is reproducible.

items.title: I can explain the purpose of a logbook and describe what it should contain
items.what: A logbook is a complete, chronological record of an experiment. It should include dates and times of entries, all raw data, the step-by-step method, diagrams of the apparatus, any errors or unexpected events, calculations, and conclusions.
items.why: A logbook authenticates the data generated in an experiment. It allows the experimenter to verify their own results later, enables other researchers to reproduce the work, and provides a transparent record of how and when data was collected.
items.example: If a student records that their voltmeter malfunctioned partway through a trial and was replaced with a different model, this logbook entry allows future experimenters to understand a potential source of inconsistency in the data.

items.title: I can identify actions that would make an experiment invalid
items.what: An experiment becomes invalid when more than one independent variable is changed at once, when controlled variables are allowed to shift during trials, when personal error affects data collection, or when data is selectively reported without acknowledgement.
items.why: Each of these actions breaks the logic of the experiment. If the cause of a change in the dependent variable cannot be isolated to the independent variable, no valid conclusion can be drawn.
items.example: If a student changes both the length and the mass of a pendulum between trials to 'save time', the results cannot tell them which variable is responsible for any change in the period.
